title: ABOUT PFIZER
summary: Pfizer is a Delaware-incorporated global biopharmaceutical company founded in 1942, focused on discovering, developing, manufacturing and commercializing medicines and vaccines worldwide. It aims to improve health and expand access to affordable care, emphasizing patient value, outcomes, access and responsible pricing. Its purpose is “Breakthroughs that change patients’ lives,” supported by pipeline advancement, marketed products and responsible capital deployment. 2026 priorities are maximizing transaction value, delivering R&D milestones, investing in post-2028 growth and scaling AI. Pfizer pursues growth through its pipeline, existing products and business development, including the Metsera and Seagen acquisitions and 2025 YaoPharma and 3SBio licensing agreements; it is expanding AI across R&D, manufacturing, commercial operations and patient engagement.

title: COMMERCIAL OPERATIONS
summary: Pfizer’s global operations comprise Biopharma, PC1 (contract development/manufacturing and specialty API supply), and Pfizer Ignite (R&D services for selected biotech companies); Ignite is being discontinued, and Biopharma is the sole reportable segment. Biopharma’s 2025 commercial divisions were U.S. and International. From January 2026, its structure adds Global Hospital and Biosimilars, with defined geographic and product responsibilities. The text outlines 2026 product areas and examples across Primary Care, Specialty Care, Oncology, and Hospital and Biosimilars, and directs readers to financial notes, MD&A, and risk-factor disclosures for further information.

title: RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
summary: R&D aims to translate science into impactful medicines and vaccines, improve existing products, and explore new indications. Priorities are differentiated therapies, long-term research capabilities, and flexible partnerships. Focus areas include oncology, internal medicine, vaccines, and inflammation/immunology; external collaborations, licenses, acquisitions, and investments supplement internal research and share expertise, costs, and risks. A unified, end-to-end organization oversees R&D, with portfolio management allocating resources; savings are expected to be reinvested. Spending is not reported by phase or therapeutic area because it is managed collectively and can shift. The text also describes the lengthy, uncertain development pipeline, points to candidate and filing details and expense disclosures elsewhere, and references R&D risks.

title: COLLABORATION AND CO-PROMOTION AGREEMENTS
summary: Pfizer describes collaboration and co-promotion arrangements supporting R&D, sales and distribution. Comirnaty is jointly developed and commercialized with BioNTech, with equal development costs and gross-profit sharing, subject to territory exclusions and approvals. Eliquis is partnered with BMS, with study-dependent development costs, generally equal profit/loss sharing and market-specific arrangements. Xtandi is partnered with Astellas, with U.S. equal profit, loss and certain cost sharing, plus tiered international royalties. Orgovyx is partnered with SMPS for equal U.S. profit and allowable-expense sharing; the relugolix combination-tablet collaboration ended in December 2024. Padcev is jointly developed and commercialized with Astellas: U.S. sales, promotion, distribution and cost/profit sharing are specified, while international rights and profit-sharing mechanisms vary by territory. Takeda commercializes Adcetris outside Pfizer’s U.S., territories and Canada rights, paying tiered royalties. Tivdak is partnered with Genmab, with promotion rights and Pfizer’s profit, royalty and expense arrangements varying by indication and territory; Zai Lab has rights in specified Asian markets. Other product and pipeline collaborations also exist. Related revenues generally appear in Alliance revenues, except certain direct sales and most Comirnaty and Padcev revenues, which are Product revenues. Further information is cited in the Business, Risk Factors, MD&A and financial-statement notes.

title: International Operations, Sales and Marketing
summary: The company supplies medicines and vaccines to about 200 countries, views emerging markets as growth opportunities, and reports international revenue shares, major markets and countries exceeding revenue thresholds for 2023–2025; it also notes risks inherent in global operations. Products are sold through wholesalers and other healthcare channels, with vaccines sold to government and institutional buyers, including contracts subject to change. Sales efforts include formulary access, rebates, disease-management support, lawful promotion to providers, patients and payors, consumer and public-health advertising, patient assistance, discounted medicines through TrumpRx.gov, and virtual and in-person customer engagement.

title: PATENTS AND OTHER INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS
summary: Pfizer describes its patent, co-promotion and licensing rights, how patent terms and regulatory exclusivity vary by country, and limitations on protection internationally. It lists basic patent expiration years for major products in the U.S., Europe and Japan, with notes on pending extensions, challenges, approvals, collaborations and commercialization rights. It explains that loss of exclusivity can trigger lower-priced generic or biosimilar competition, materially reduce revenues—particularly from 2026–2030—and may involve third-party infringement claims; Pfizer defends its rights while considering patient access. It also describes renewable trademark and trade-dress protections.

title: COMPETITION
summary: Pfizer competes in highly regulated markets on efficacy, safety, usability and cost against global and specialist biopharma firms, generics and biosimilars. Competitors’ R&D, patent challenges and product launches can erode sales or make products obsolete. Pfizer responds with substantial R&D and business development, ongoing research and education, stronger launches, organizational adaptation, and affordability and access programs, including Accord for a Healthier World. Vaccines face alternative and next-generation products; biosimilars compete with biologics and Pfizer seeks early market entry. Generics can enter after patent or exclusivity loss, often at lower prices, benefit from streamlined approvals and payer or pharmacy substitution policies; China’s QCE and VBP programs intensify pressure. Biosimilars are highly similar, lower-cost biologics, regulated through FDA and EU EMA pathways.

title: PRICING PRESSURES AND MANAGED CARE ORGANIZATIONS
summary: The text describes commercial healthcare cost pressures, including high-deductible plans, utilization controls, insurer and PBM bargaining, rebates, competitive markets, and purchaser discount demands. Pfizer’s responses include advocacy, affordability and access initiatives, engagement with payors and authorities, and evidence of product value. It explains how MCO consolidation and formularies, protocols, tiers, and exclusions affect prices, patient costs, product use, and revenues, alongside evolving payment reforms and scrutiny of PBMs. It also reports a September 2025 U.S. government agreement on international price comparisons, discounted TrumpRx.gov sales, and a conditional three-year Section 232 tariff grace period tied to U.S. manufacturing investment; final agreements are pending.

title: RAW MATERIALS
summary: The company sources essential raw materials from numerous global suppliers, generally in sufficient quantities and often from multiple sources. It does not expect availability to significantly affect 2026 operations, but monitors potential disruptions from geopolitical and trade negotiations that could affect costs. Mitigation measures include active supplier management, qualifying additional suppliers, and advance purchasing where possible.

title: GOVERNMENT REGULATION AND PRICE CONSTRAINTS

nodes.title: Biosimilar Regulation
nodes.summary: The company faces extensive, costly government regulation across its markets covering biopharmaceutical development and sales, pricing, healthcare interactions, patient assistance, research, privacy, and security; violations can trigger penalties, operational restrictions, product actions, approval delays, and reputational harm. In the U.S., FDA and other agencies regulate products and activities before and after marketing. Drugs and biologics require NDA/BLA approval based on safety and efficacy; sponsors may have post-approval study, adverse-event reporting, pharmacovigilance, manufacturing-quality, supply-chain-tracing, and promotion obligations. Emergency Use Authorizations permit conditional use during declared emergencies but require supporting data, ongoing compliance, and efforts toward full approval. Biosimilars must be highly similar without clinically meaningful differences; interchangeability permits pharmacy substitution in many states. Applications may be filed four years after reference licensure and approved after 12 years; another interchangeable cannot be approved until one year after the first.

nodes.title: Sales and Marketing Regulations
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s sales and marketing are subject to federal and state healthcare fraud, abuse, false-claims, consumer-protection, and advertising laws, covering both consumer and provider marketing. The Anti-Kickback Statute bars value exchanged to generate federally reimbursable business; the Civil Monetary Penalties Law penalizes various violations, including kickbacks and causing false claims; and the False Claims Act prohibits knowingly submitting or causing fraudulent payment claims, including false legal-compliance certifications. Governments also regulate and require disclosure of manufacturer interactions with providers and academic medical centers and mandate compliance programs; state attorneys general have pursued prescription-drug marketing under consumer-protection and false-advertising laws.

nodes.title: Pricing, Reimbursement and Access Regulations
nodes.summary: The text reviews regulatory and policy risks to Pfizer’s pricing, reimbursement, access, and operations. It covers U.S. MFN initiatives and Pfizer’s 2025 agreement, discounted TrumpRx sales and a conditional tariff grace period; government rebates, price reporting, IRA Part D redesign and Medicare drug-price negotiations affecting named products; potential changes to Medicaid, 340B, Medicare Part B reimbursement, state formularies, advisory recommendations, importation, price controls, and payer practices. It describes ongoing 340B policy disputes, litigation, and oversight, plus anti-corruption and evolving privacy, cybersecurity, and AI-related obligations. Outside the U.S., it outlines medicines-approval authorities and procedures in the EU, U.K., Japan, China, and other markets, and the proposed EU Pharma Package and other legislative initiatives that could affect Pfizer.

nodes.title: Regulatory, Pricing, Anti-Corruption and Data Privacy Risks
nodes.summary: The text describes legal challenges to state 340B contract-pharmacy laws and potential effects of federal or state developments on Pfizer’s 340B integrity initiative and obligations. It covers Medicaid cost controls, rebates, formularies, advisory committee recommendations, and expanding government scrutiny and regulation of drug prices and access—including importation, reference pricing, caps, discounts, penalties, and price disclosures. Commercial payors may follow Medicare policies, favor generics and biosimilars, and face industry consolidation. It also summarizes anti-corruption laws covering foreign officials and some healthcare professionals, and evolving privacy and data-security requirements, cross-border conflicts, AI-related data use, rising enforcement and litigation, and potential penalties and reputational harm from noncompliance or breaches.

nodes.title: New Drug Approvals
nodes.summary: The text outlines global medicine approval systems and regulators, the pending EU Pharma Package reform and other EU legislative initiatives, and EU and international pharmacovigilance requirements. It describes government pricing and reimbursement controls, with emphasis on China’s negotiations, reimbursement lists, generic tenders, and uncertain future effects; healthcare-provider disclosure rules; global patent protections and continuing IP challenges; evolving privacy, data-use, AI, and cybersecurity compliance risks; and environmental-law compliance spending and cleanup of legacy contamination.

nodes.title: Pharmaceutical Regulation, Pricing, IP and Privacy
nodes.summary: The page outlines evolving EU pharmaceutical and digital legislation and pharmacovigilance oversight. It describes government pricing and reimbursement controls worldwide, with detailed discussion of China’s negotiations, reimbursement lists, volume-based procurement and cost-containment measures. It covers disclosure requirements for transfers of value to healthcare providers, global patent protections and challenges, and extensive, changing privacy rules governing sensitive health data, cross-border use, AI, enforcement, cybersecurity risks and potential penalties.

summary: Covers extensive U.S. and international regulation of drug development, approval, manufacturing, safety monitoring, biosimilars, marketing, healthcare-provider interactions, fraud and anti-corruption, and patient assistance. Reviews pricing, reimbursement and access controls—including U.S. Medicare, Medicaid and 340B policies, negotiations, rebates, tariffs, importation and price limits; commercial payer practices; and China’s procurement and reimbursement systems. Also addresses EU and other regulatory reforms, disclosure rules, patent protections and disputes, privacy, cybersecurity and AI obligations, environmental compliance, and the operational, financial and reputational consequences of noncompliance.

title: ENVIRONMENTAL MATTERS
summary: Pfizer complies with environmental laws and remediates contamination from past industrial activities. In 2025, it spent about $125 million on environmental capital expenditures and $188 million on other environmental expenses; future compliance costs are not expected to materially affect capital spending or financial position. Pfizer targets net-zero emissions by 2040, reducing its own GHG emissions 95% and value-chain emissions 90% from 2019 levels, through reduction plans and supplier goals. 2025 plan-related spending was not material; future costs and long-term financial effects remain uncertain, and Pfizer monitors them. Climate-related risks are discussed in its Risk Factors section.

summary: Pfizer describes its people strategy for approximately 75,000 employees, centered on its purpose and values and on attracting, developing, and retaining talent through supportive culture, flexible work, wellness, and merit-based advancement. It covers inclusion, accountability and open communication; performance feedback, safe reporting channels, surveys, forums, and Bravo recognition; leadership and project-based work; learning and career growth, including AI and technology skills; global EHS policies, training, audits, and well-being support; and annual global pay equity analysis based on role, education, experience, performance, and location.

title: ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS
summary: The section outlines material business risks, noting that the factors listed are not exhaustive or fully predictable and must be considered alongside the report and other SEC filings. The business also faces general risks, including economic conditions, geopolitical events, extreme weather, and natural disasters. Materialization of known or unknown risks could harm operations, financial condition and results, cash flows, prospects, reputation, or credit ratings, now or in the future. The discussion includes forward-looking statements.

title: RISKS RELATED TO OUR BUSINESS, INDUSTRY AND OPERATIONS:

nodes.title: MANAGED CARE TRENDS
nodes.summary: Consolidated private payors, PBMs, and governments increasingly use rebates, fees, formularies, cost sharing, utilization controls, exclusions, and value- or indication-based pricing to contain drug costs, creating risks to timely, adequate, value-reflective pricing and coverage. Patient-assistance restrictions, higher out-of-pocket costs, and administrative barriers can delay or deter treatment and shift consumers toward cheaper, generic, or direct-purchase options. Further consolidation and public IRA prices may intensify pricing pressure and rebate demands. Payor arrangements also face government scrutiny, changing fraud-and-abuse safe harbors, and evolving legal and industry guidance.

nodes.title: COMPETITIVE PRODUCTS
nodes.summary: The text outlines Pfizer’s risks from competition, including new and global rivals, pricing and contracting pressures, generics, biosimilars, patent challenges, early launches, and U.S. drug-pricing agreements; these may reduce sales. Revenue is concentrated in major products and customers, exposing results to exclusivity losses, demand, safety, regulatory, pricing, supply, litigation, publicity, and market changes, including COVID-product declines and concentrated acquisitions. It also describes the need for sustained R&D and the risks of rising costs and regulation, trial and quality issues, candidate failure, poor investment choices, changing markets, and uncertain reimbursement or commercial success.

nodes.title: Competition, Revenue Concentration, and R&D Risks
nodes.summary: The page describes generic and biosimilar competition, including patent challenges, at-risk launches, pricing pressure, and reimbursement barriers. It notes that 12 products generated 65% of 2025 revenue, exposing results to product, patent, safety, regulatory, market, and supply risks; upcoming exclusivity losses, concentrated investments, declining COVID-19 product sales, and reliance on major customers add uncertainty. It also outlines the need for ongoing R&D and the risks of high costs, trial and regulatory challenges, candidate failures, poor investment choices, and changing markets.

nodes.summary: Outlines risks from global economic, political, regulatory, trade, tariff, currency, interest-rate and public-health conditions, including emerging-market instability, government pricing controls, and potential tariff impacts and related U.S. investment commitments. Describes foreign-exchange exposure and effects on revenues, costs, assets, pensions and financial guidance. Covers supply, manufacturing, distribution, sales and marketing disruptions; capacity, quality and third-party manufacturing challenges; regulatory inspections and compliance consequences; and nitrosamine assessments, potential market actions, and Chantix’s recall and return to market.

nodes.title: Third-Party Reliance and Counterfeit Product Risks
key_items: COLLABORATIONS AND OTHER RELATIONSHIPS WITH THIRD PARTIES
nodes.summary: The company relies on collaborators, vendors, CROs, and other partners for research, development, manufacturing, commercialization, and outsourced services, while lacking control over many activities. Upfront transaction costs, partner failures, disruptions, noncompliance, or relationship terminations may delay or harm products, revenues, quality, compliance, and reputation. Counterfeit medicines threaten patient safety, trust, sales, and may cause recalls or litigation; online pharmacies and e-commerce increase exposure, with counterfeiting observed across several portfolios. The company invests in education, detection technologies, supply monitoring and interdiction, and policy advocacy, but these efforts may not prevent the threat from growing.

summary: The section covers risks from payor consolidation and cost-control practices that can restrict coverage, raise patient costs, and pressure prices, alongside evolving legal scrutiny. Competition from new products, generics, biosimilars, patent challenges, and pricing agreements may erode sales; revenue concentration, exclusivity losses, changing demand, and uncertain R&D outcomes add exposure. It also addresses global economic, political, currency, trade, and tariff risks; manufacturing, supply, quality, regulatory, and product-specific issues; reliance on third parties; and counterfeit medicines despite mitigation efforts.

title: RISKS RELATED TO GOVERNMENT REGULATION AND LEGAL PROCEEDINGS:

nodes.title: PRICING AND REIMBURSEMENT
nodes.summary: Government pricing, reimbursement, coverage, and access regulations could reduce Pfizer’s revenues in the U.S. and internationally. U.S. pressures include ACA subsidy and Medicaid funding changes, IRA price negotiations and inflation rebates, CMMI models, state measures, generic competition, and the 2025 MFN initiatives, MFN Agreement, and TrumpRx discounts, all carrying pricing, access, demand, and competitive risks. Eliquis, Ibrance, Xtandi, and Xeljanz have been selected for Medicare price-setting; further selections and legal challenges add uncertainty. Consolidation among pharmacies, wholesalers, and PBMs may intensify pressure. Abroad, government controls, China tenders, EU pharmaceutical reform and health-technology assessments, and vaccine tender competition may constrain prices and access or affect sales.

nodes.title: U.S. HEALTHCARE REGULATION
nodes.summary: U.S. healthcare regulation is highly changeable. The 2025 OBBBA cuts to Medicaid, marketplaces, and Medicare payments are projected to reduce federal spending and increase the uninsured population, potentially lowering product demand and increasing price controls. Further federal and state reforms could affect the business through budget cuts, patent and importation rules, reimbursement and international reference pricing, FDA disclosure of confidential information, limits on healthcare-professional interactions and advertising, and cost-focused comparative effectiveness. Vaccine-policy changes create additional risks, including evolving requirements, investigations, policy and liability changes, delays or loss of approvals, recommendations, coverage or reimbursement, and agency changes; in January 2026, CDC reduced routinely recommended childhood immunizations. Additional cuts to Medicare, Medicaid, other public programs, and 340B could reduce product payments and harm results. IRA implementation remains under evaluation; MFN initiatives and proposed mandatory CMMI pilots may require further concessions. Commercial payors may follow Medicare restrictions, and coverage and reimbursement can worsen even after initially favorable decisions.

nodes.title: DEVELOPMENT, REGULATORY APPROVAL AND MARKETING OF PRODUCTS
nodes.summary: Drug, vaccine, and biologic development is costly, lengthy, risky, and uncertain. Risks include trial recruitment or candidate failures, changing data or regulatory feedback, protocol amendments and added studies, missed milestones, inability to address regulator comments, and inconsistent FDA decisions. Approval and commercial prospects depend on safety, efficacy, regulatory interpretations, emergency or accelerated pathways, advisory recommendations, labeling, populations, manufacturing, and post-approval conditions. Adverse concerns or administrative decisions can reduce sales or coverage, trigger assessments, litigation, recalls, or withdrawals, as with Oxbryta. Additional requirements may delay or prevent expected approvals.

nodes.title: POST-AUTHORIZATION/APPROVAL DATA
nodes.summary: FDA approval may require or sponsors may undertake post-marketing studies, whose results and other emerging safety data can lead to withdrawn approval, label changes, or safety and efficacy concerns. Similar but differing international regulations can create uncertainty across markets, and concerns about one product may affect its entire class; implications may not be immediately clear. Oxbryta was voluntarily withdrawn worldwide in September 2024 after its overall benefit was judged not to outweigh risk. In October 2025, the EMA recommended its authorization remain suspended following a negative benefit-risk opinion; Pfizer’s engagement with the FDA is ongoing.

nodes.title: LEGAL MATTERS
nodes.summary: Pfizer faces diverse and unpredictable legal proceedings, including patent, product liability, commercial, securities, antitrust, employment, environmental, tax and other claims, which may cause significant adverse financial effects. Patent losses could remove product protection and reduce sales. Government investigations and qui tam suits may bring fines, criminal charges, business restrictions, agreements, penalties and reputational harm. Extensive regulation of marketing, pricing and healthcare interactions, evolving enforcement, information demands and claims create compliance and reputational risks, potentially heightened by AI and digital marketing. Legal and environmental liabilities require uncertain estimates; accrued amounts may not cover future costs. Further details appear in Note 16A.

summary: Government pricing, reimbursement, coverage, and regulatory changes in the U.S. and abroad—including Medicare negotiations, Medicaid and other program cuts, MFN initiatives, EU reforms, tenders, and payer consolidation—may constrain prices, access, and demand. Healthcare policy and vaccine-policy changes could alter approvals, recommendations, coverage, and payments. Product development, trials, approvals, and post-approval safety monitoring are costly and uncertain; adverse findings or regulatory actions may change labeling, restrict or withdraw products, or impair sales. Pfizer also faces varied litigation, investigations, compliance, patent, environmental, and other liabilities that may cause financial, operational, and reputational harm.

title: RISKS RELATED TO INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY, TECHNOLOGY AND SECURITY:
summary: Pfizer warns that inadequate or challenged patent, trademark, trade-secret, copyright and other IP protections, changing laws, country-specific rules, compulsory licensing, disputes, and loss of third-party licenses could enable imitation, generic or biosimilar competition, reduce exclusivity and harm results. It faces patent challenges, damages suits, infringement claims and risky early launches; outcomes may delay or block products, require royalties or damages, or end sales. Cyberattacks, IT outages, vendor and supply-chain vulnerabilities, and data breaches could cause operational, legal, financial and reputational harm despite controls and insurance. AI use may not deliver expected benefits and brings uncertain regulation, unreliable or biased outputs and data, IP and confidentiality concerns, compliance and liability risks, and dependence on few providers.

Pfizer Global Supply oversees 36 manufacturing plants and distribution facilities worldwide; U.S. R&D facilities total about 7 million square feet, while labs in the U.K., India, and Belgium are leased. Blackstone’s 2025–2028 arrangement may provide up to $326 million; $102 million reduced 2025 R&D expense, with approval milestones up to $277 million and sales milestones up to $897 million. Funding is treated as an obligation to provide services and reduces R&D expense over related cost periods. For the first two arrangements, approval- and sales-based milestones are recorded as intangible assets and amortized over the shorter of agreement term or product commercial life; liability interest accretion is interest expense. Separate R&D efficiency initiatives, expanded in early 2025, are expected to cost $600 million through 2026, all for Biopharma; most was recorded in 2025, with cash outlays mainly in 2025–2026. Phase one focuses mainly on operational efficiencies, is expected to cost about $1.4 billion—primarily Biopharma severance and implementation cash expenses—and had incurred $1.1 billion through December 31, 2025, including $875 million in restructuring charges. A 2023–2025 reconciliation details changes in gross unrecognized benefits and their balance-sheet classifications, with explanatory notes on prior-period positions, settlements, payments, foreign exchange and statute expirations. Totals reflect unamortized discounts, premiums, and issuance costs. The company had a $7.0 billion U.S. revolving facility maturing October 2030, available for general purposes and commercial-paper support, plus $237 million in lender credit lines, mostly expiring within a year; essentially all were unused at year-end 2025.

nodes.title: D. Long-Term Debt

The company details 2025 U.S. dollar and euro note issuances, coupons, maturities, principal, redemption terms, uses of proceeds, effective rates, and guarantees by finance subsidiaries PNIF and PIE. It also describes PIE’s 2023 $31 billion Seagen acquisition financing and the 2025 redemption of $3 billion of its 2026 notes.

It reports derivative fair values and notional amounts for 2024–2025; gains and losses recognized, reclassified, or amortized through earnings and OCI; forecast inventory-sale hedge amounts, expected future reclassification, and hedge duration; foreign-currency debt used in net-investment hedges; and cumulative fair-value hedge adjustments and carrying amounts for long-term debt.

nodes.title: F. Credit Risk

title: Amended and Restated January 2025

nodes.title: SECTION 1. PURPOSE
nodes.summary: The Pfizer Inc. Global Performance Plan, amended and restated effective January 1, 2025, aims to build a culture of high performance and attract, motivate, and engage committed colleagues who help achieve the Company’s annual financial, strategic, and operational goals.

nodes.title: SECTION 2. DEFINITIONS
nodes.summary: Defines the Plan’s key terms, including covered entities and personnel; Awards, incentive pools, targets, opportunities, earnings and performance periods; Company leadership and governing bodies; compliance warnings and cause; employee eligibility and termination categories; retirement, separation and 409A concepts; and applicable laws, country groups, and executive incentive programs. It also specifies how Eligible Earnings are calculated and excluded, and assigns discretion for determining Cause and certain termination classifications.

nodes.title: SECTION 3. ADMINISTRATION
nodes.summary: The Compensation Committee or designated executives administer the Plan, with broad authority to set rules and award terms, interpret the Plan, select participants, determine targets, opportunities, goals and awards, make related determinations, and delegate authority. They act in sole discretion in the Company’s best interest, not as fiduciaries; decisions need not be uniform and are generally final and binding. The Committee may adjust awards or pool funding for extraordinary events or legal, regulatory, judicial or accounting changes, remedy Plan or award defects and inconsistencies, and adjust awards or funding when assuming awards or obligations through a business acquisition or combination.

nodes.title: SECTION 4. ELIGIBILITY
nodes.summary: Employees may be selected by the Committee or its designee to participate for a Performance Period. Employees hired after October 1 generally become eligible the following January 1, unless eligibility is waived; employees may participate in only one annual Company or Affiliate cash incentive plan, excluding those in sales or other cash incentive plans. U.S. or Puerto Rico employees receiving a Compliance Written Warning during the period are capped at the lesser of 90% of target or 90% of their pre-performance-adjustment award; those receiving an IFW are capped at the lesser of 75% of either amount.

nodes.title: SECTION 5. AWARDS
nodes.summary: The Committee grants performance-period Awards based on a target Incentive Pool, Company results against annual goals (revenue, adjusted net income, cash flow, pipeline, and other factors), allocation to business units, and individual performance. Target Awards are calculated using eligible earnings and incentive percentages or fixed amounts, with country- and program-specific rules, eligibility proration, and a protection for certain ELTI participants against reductions below their 2021 target. Final Awards are capped at 250% of target; the Committee may adjust awards for employment, compensation, eligibility, or transfer changes and to comply with law. Awards are generally paid by the 15th day of the third month after the performance year, subject to local rules, deferral, legal-compliance delays, or release requirements. Voluntary departures before period-end forfeit Awards; later departures may be eligible at Committee discretion, with a special resignation-date rule for U.S. Blueprint Leaders. Involuntary departures before period-end receive a prorated target based on eligible days and earnings, excluding nonworking notice periods, but the Company may reduce or deny payment based on forecasts and performance; any payment is made promptly and no later than March 15 of the following year.

nodes.title: Award Calculations, Payments, and Voluntary Termination
nodes.summary: Target awards based on annual incentive amounts are prorated by eligible days, and final awards are capped at 250% of target. The Committee may adjust awards for employment or compensation changes and include legally required terms. Awards are generally paid by the 15th day of the third month after the performance year, subject to local requirements, deferral rules, legal delays, or receipt of a required release after involuntary termination. Voluntary termination before the performance period ends forfeits the award; termination afterward may qualify for payment at the Committee’s discretion. For U.S. Blueprint Leaders, voluntary termination begins when resignation is tendered and the 60-day notice starts.

nodes.title: Involuntary Termination
nodes.summary: The text sets award rules for involuntary termination, cause or performance-related termination, retirement, disability or approved leave, death, and failure to sign a required restricted covenant agreement. It specifies eligibility, prorated calculations and exclusions, Company/Committee discretion to adjust or deny awards based on performance and funding, payment deadlines and conditions, treatment of military differential pay, and special retirement-date rules for U.S. Blueprint Leaders. Failure to accept required restrictive covenants generally forfeits the award.

key_items: Terminations for Cause or Performance-Related Terminations

nodes.summary: The page explains incentive-award treatment following involuntary termination, termination for cause or performance reasons, retirement, short-term disability or approved leave, and death. Eligibility, proration, payment timing, and Company or Committee discretion—including possible reduced or no awards—vary by circumstance; military differential pay includes an active-employee award calculation. Blueprint Leaders and others required to sign restrictive covenants forfeit awards if they do not accept the specified agreement on time, unless the Company decides otherwise.

nodes.title: Plan Amendments, Termination, and Award Deferrals
key_items: SECTION 9. DEFERRAL OF AWARDS UNDER THE COMPANY’S DEFERRED COMPENSATION PLAN
nodes.summary: The Company may amend or terminate the Plan at any time, including changing eligibility, funding, measures, targets, results, or terms to meet legal and local requirements; compensation remains subject to government rules. The Committee may delegate compliance actions, establish country sub-plans, and make administrative changes. The Committee or designee may amend Awards retroactively or prospectively, without participant consent, to address potential Section 409A defects. Awards may be designated for deferral under the Company’s Deferred Compensation Plan, subject to its terms and Section 409A.

nodes.title: SECTION 10. TAX CONSIDERATIONS
nodes.summary: U.S. Award payments are taxable when received, and the Company and its affiliates may withhold taxes and other authorized deductions and take steps to meet tax obligations. The Plan is intended to comply with Section 409A; the Committee may amend Awards, without participant consent, to address potential defects. The Company does not guarantee exemption from Section 409A or avoidance of related penalties, and the provision does not admit that benefits are deferred compensation. For participants outside the U.S., local tax rules govern; withholding may cover applicable income, social insurance, payroll, fringe-benefit, and other tax-related items.

nodes.title: SECTION 11. RECOUPMENT
nodes.summary: The section permits recoupment under Pfizer’s policy after significant financial restatements (excluding accounting-principle changes), if awards would have been lower or unavailable, subject to law and review of relevant circumstances; this is in addition to other remedies and does not limit recovery from any employee under applicable law, including Exchange Act Section 10D. Awards exempt from Section 409A may be offset against participants’ debts to the Company or affiliates. Awards are also subject to other applicable recoupment policies and restrictive covenants; violations may lead to unvested-award cancellation, recovery of shares, cash, withholding taxes or sale proceeds, or other Committee-selected remedies.

nodes.title: SECTION 12. GENERAL PROVISIONS
nodes.summary: Awards are discretionary variable compensation, not guaranteed or part of an employment or service contract; employees have no entitlement to awards or consistent treatment, and the Company may terminate the Plan or employment/service at any time without severance liability. Recipients generally need only provide services. Invalid provisions are conformed to law or severed, preserving the remainder. The Committee may adapt awards for foreign participants and impose tax-equalization conditions; it may treat certain leaves as continuous employment, subject to Section 409A separation rules.

nodes.title: SECTION 13. GOVERNING LAW
nodes.summary: Section 13 provides that the Plan is governed, construed, regulated, and administered under New York law, disregarding conflict-of-law principles except where controlling federal law supersedes it. The text also lists Group 1 countries, where monthly daily earnings and targets accumulate: Australia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bolivia, Brazil, Bulgaria, Canada, Chile, China, Colombia, Cyprus, Costa Rica, Croatia, Czech Republic, Denmark, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Estonia, Finland, France, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Kazakhstan, Korea, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malaysia, Mexico, Netherlands, New Zealand, Nicaragua, Norway, Panama, Pakistan, Paraguay, Philippines, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Russian Federation, Serbia, Singapore, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Taiwan, and Thailand.

nodes.title: 1. Deferral Election for Cash Compensation.
nodes.summary: Non-employee Pfizer directors may elect by written notice to the Company Secretary, by year-end, to defer all or a specified portion of fees for the following year and subsequent years until separation from service. The election continues until separation unless ended for future fees by timely written notice, effective the next calendar year. Previously credited amounts are unaffected and remain payable under the Plan’s applicable provisions, including its death provision.

nodes.title: 2. Investment of Deferred Cash Compensation.
nodes.summary: Deferred cash compensation is held in the Company’s general funds and credited to each director’s account. At the director’s election, the account earns monthly compounded interest at 120% of the Long-Term Applicable Federal Rate, receives units based on deferred fees divided by the Company stock closing price at quarter-end, or reflects gains and losses from other alternatives selected by Pfizer. Directors may change the investment form by notifying the Plan administrator, but switches involving Pfizer-stock-denominated accounts are restricted if a switch involving specified Company or plan stock accounts occurred in the preceding six months. Awarded Units are unaffected except as provided in paragraph 3(C).

nodes.title: 3. Awards of Units.
nodes.summary: Directors receive unit awards upon first election and annually thereafter, adjusted for stock changes. Until ownership guidelines are met, awards remain credited; eligible directors may elect annual deferral until separation or prompt payment in shares, with later elections changing only future awards. Six months after separation, directors may switch investment alternatives. Employer-imposed compensation limits may reduce unit awards, permit cash-pay reductions, or substitute interest-bearing account credits; restricted credits cannot be redirected or earn dividends. Excess value may be donated to charities selected by the Governance Committee.

nodes.title: 4. Dividends.
nodes.summary: Dividends generally increase a director’s account units based on cash or stock dividends, with adjustments for changes such as stock splits. Directors may elect cash dividends instead of deferred credits under different rules for pre-2005 and post-2004 awards, including deadlines, Section 409A conditions, and permanent elections; special transition rules apply to awards through 2008. For compensation and units granted, earned, and vested before 2005, directors may elect payment in cash or shares as a lump sum or 2–15 annual installments, with specified start dates, by electing or changing the election at least one year before leaving; absent an election, payment starts the following year in five installments. The text begins the rules for post-2004 deferred compensation but does not provide their terms.

nodes.title: Awarded Unit Dividends and Distribution Elections
key_items: (A) Deferred Cash Compensation and Awarded Units deferred prior to January 1, 2005.
nodes.summary: The text provides for adjusting credited units after stock splits other than stock dividends. It describes cash-dividend elections for awarded units before and after 2004, including deadlines, Section 409A rules, and when elections are permanent. For deferred compensation and units granted, earned, and vested before 2005, directors may elect at least a year before leaving to receive accounts in cash or shares, as a lump sum or 2–15 annual installments, with specified payment timing; absent an election, payment is made in five annual installments beginning the following year.

nodes.title: (B) Deferred Cash Compensation and Awarded Units deferred after December 31, 2004.
nodes.summary: For post-2004 deferred cash compensation, awarded units, and earnings, directors generally elect distribution timing and form within 30 days of eligibility; certain pre-2009 eligible directors had a 2008 transition deadline. Elections are irrevocable, with annual elections from 2022 onward applying only to the following year’s deferrals. Directors choose when payments start after separation and either a lump sum or 2–15 installments; defaults are the following year and five installments. Account values use the relevant common-stock closing price, and installments divide the remaining balance equally. Key employees face a six-month payment delay after separation, subject to earlier death. Eligible 2009 distribution amounts could be elected for a one-time July 1, 2009 lump-sum payment.

nodes.title: 6. Death.
nodes.summary: The provisions allow directors to designate, change, or cancel death beneficiaries by written notice to the Company Secretary; absent a surviving designation, payment goes to the estate representative. Pre-2005 deferred compensation and vested units, with earnings, are paid in a lump sum as soon as practicable after death. For post-2004 amounts, directors may elect a beneficiary lump sum or 2–15 installments under specified Section 409A deadlines; qualifying pre-2009 directors had a transition deadline, and elections are irrevocable. Account rights cannot be assigned, and the Company may ignore assignments. The Plan is to comply with Section 409A and defines Key Employee and Separation from Service. Post-2004 deferrals may be re-elected only subject to 12-month waiting and advance-notice rules and a five-year minimum delay.

nodes.title: Assignment Restrictions and Section 409A Compliance
nodes.summary: Directors may not assign rights to deferred cash compensation, awarded units, or related earnings; the Company may disregard an assignment and pay as if none occurred. The Plan is to be interpreted and administered, to the extent permitted, in compliance with Section 409A. It defines a Key Employee under the applicable tax-code rules, determined each January 1 and effective for the following 12 months, and defines Separation from Service by reference to Section 409A.

nodes.title: 9. Re-Deferrals.
nodes.summary: Directors may make subsequent elections to change the timing or form of distributions from Post-2004 deferred compensation accounts. Each election must take effect at least 12 months after it is made, be made at least 12 months before the scheduled distribution or first installment, and delay the distribution or first installment by at least five years from its original scheduled date.
